doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Household jazz and David Baker, big brother and dean of jazz education
summary: Parents' Ellington and Basie records, supportive local musicians, and David Baker, roommate at Yale and pioneer of jazz pedagogy.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Was jazz, before this seeing Ray Brown, was jazz part of your household?

Oh yes. My parents were into Duke Ellington, Count Basie. My mother’s youngest brother was into the more current stuff like with the bebop and stuff like that. And all these musicians around town, you know, like were all very supportive. There are so many names I hesitate to name a lot of names, but I mentioned the main ones like the Montgomery brothers and David Baker. David Baker was there and he is a few years older than me but he’s like my big brother and he’s always looked out for me. In fact when I went to Yale University we were roommates. And my mother always told him, said, “David now you make sure that he studies.” David and I roomed and we had bunk beds. And David used to always pull me out of the bed and I have to say that David Baker is one of the — I’m fortunate to have a brother like him. Even though we’re not blood brothers we are brothers. Because he has taken care of me since I was a young guy and he’s always been there for me and he’s always encouraged me, and he’s a phenomenal person. You know when they start talking about who’s the dean of jazz education, it’s David Baker. Because he was one of the first — he and Jerry Coker were one of the first guys, and then John Mehegen came along with his books trying to define and articulate in a codified way, improvisation. Because most of what we learned, I mean we used to transcribe guys’ solos and try to figure out how they were doing this over the chords and this, that and the other. But David was one of the first to start putting this in a form that was accessible to teach how to play jazz and Jerry too. Jerry is a very dear friend too. And then Jamie Aebersold came in as a freshman at Indiana University when I was there, and David was there, and that’s how he got his start. Because he was a protege of David Baker also.
Can you imagine that any of them could envision where that led? You know this gathering here is astounding to me.

Well that’s what’s so beautiful about it. We were dealing with it as a labor of love not particularly knowing which way it was going to go. And I was very fortunate to be involved early on, as David refers to one of the Renaissance men of trying to get jazz in. When I went to Indiana University, 1955, I saw how the European art form and classical players were moving in and out doing their gigs and coming back to the university to teach. And I said if the seed was planted then, I said someday I’m going to try to do what © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
